units.zh: 史萬歲
units.en: Shi Wansui
units.literal: Shi Wansui

units.zh: 候騎曰：「是也．」達頭聞之，懼而引去．萬歲馳追百餘里乃及，擊大破之，斬數千級，逐北入磧數百里，虜遁逃而還．楊素害其功，因譖萬歲云：「突厥本降，初不為寇，來於塞上畜牧耳．」遂寢其功．萬歲數抗表陳狀，上未之悟．會上從仁壽宮初還京師，廢皇太子，窮東宮黨與．上問萬歲所在，萬歲實在朝堂，楊素見上方怒，因曰：「萬歲謁東宮矣．」以激怒上．上謂為信然，令召萬歲．時所將士卒在朝稱冤者數百人，萬歲謂之曰：「吾今日為汝極言於上，事當決矣．」既見上，言將士有功，為朝廷所抑，詞氣憤厲，忤於上．上大怒，令左右摧殺之．既而悔，追之不及，因下詔罪萬歲曰：「柱國、太平公萬歲，拔擢委任，每總戎機．往以南寧逆亂，令其出討．而昆州刺史爨翫包藏逆心，為民興患．朕備有成敕，令將入朝．萬歲乃多受金銀，違敕令住，致爨翫尋為反逆，更勞師旅，方始平定．所司檢校，罪合極刑，捨過念功，恕其性命，年月未久，即復本官．近復總戎，進討蕃裔．突厥達頭可汗領其兇眾，欲相拒抗，既見軍威，便即奔退，兵不血刃，賊徒瓦解．如此稱捷，國家盛事，朕欲成其勳庸，復加褒賞．而萬歲、定和通簿之日，乃懷姦詐，妄稱逆面交兵，不以實陳，懷反覆之方，弄國家之法．若竭誠立節，心無虛罔者，乃為良將，至如萬歲，懷詐要功，便是國賊，朝憲難虧，不可再捨．」死之日，天下士庶聞者，識與不識，莫不冤惜．
units.en: The scouts said, “It is he.” When Tatou heard this he withdrew in fear. Wansui galloped after them for more than a hundred li, overtook them, and broke them utterly, taking several thousand heads. He drove the fugitives north into the desert for hundreds of li before they escaped and he returned. Yang Su, jealous of his glory, slandered him: “The Turks had already surrendered and were only pasturing livestock at the border—they were not raiding.” His merit was buried. Wansui memorialized again and again; the emperor would not see it. When the emperor returned from Renshou Palace to the capital, deposed the crown prince, and hunted the eastern palace faction, he asked where Wansui was. Wansui was in fact at court, but Yang Su, seeing his anger, said, “Wansui has gone to the eastern palace,” to inflame him further. The emperor believed it and summoned Wansui. Several hundred soldiers he had commanded were at court petitioning that they had been wronged. Wansui told them, “Today I will speak out for you before the emperor—the matter will be settled.” Before the emperor he spoke of his men’s merit and how the court had suppressed them; his tone was fierce and he gave offense. The emperor raged and ordered his attendants to kill him on the spot. He soon regretted it but could not undo the deed, and issued an edict condemning Wansui: “The pillar of state and duke of Taiping, Wansui, was raised and entrusted with every campaign. When the south rebelled he was sent to punish them. Cuan Wan of Kunzhou harbored treachery and harmed the people. We had made full plans to bring him to court. Wansui took much gold and silver, disobeyed Our plan by leaving him, and Cuan Wan soon rebelled again, costing fresh armies before order returned. The crime merited death; remembering his merit We spared him and soon restored his rank. Recently he commanded the advance against the frontier tribes. Tatou led his fierce horde to resist; at sight of our might they fled—blades unstained, the enemy dissolved. Such a victory is the state’s glory; We meant to crown his merit with new rewards. Yet on the day the registers were filed he and Dinghe lied, claiming they had met the enemy in battle when they had not, mocking the laws of the state. Only one who serves with full loyalty and no deceit is a true general; Wansui, who sought merit by fraud, is a traitor. The statutes cannot bend—we will not spare him again.” On the day he died, all who heard, whether they knew him or not, mourned him.
units.literal: The scouts said: 'It is he.' When Tatou heard this he was afraid and withdrew. Wansui galloped in pursuit for more than a hundred li before overtaking them, struck a great defeat, and took several thousand heads. He drove the fleeing enemy north into the desert for several hundred li, then the barbarians escaped and he returned. Yang Su, jealous of his merit, slandered Wansui, saying: 'The Turks had originally surrendered and were not raiding at all—they had only come to pasture livestock at the border.' His merit was therefore suppressed. Wansui repeatedly submitted memorials stating the facts, but the Emperor did not understand. When the Emperor had just returned from Renshou Palace to the capital, deposed the Crown Prince, and pursued the Eastern Palace faction, he asked where Wansui was. Wansui was in fact at court, but Yang Su, seeing the Emperor's anger, said: 'Wansui has gone to visit the Eastern Palace'—to inflame him further. The Emperor believed it and ordered Wansui summoned. Several hundred soldiers he had commanded were at court petitioning that they had been wronged. Wansui told them: 'Today I shall speak out fully for you before the Emperor—the matter will be settled.' When he saw the Emperor he spoke of the troops' merit and how the court had suppressed them; his tone was fierce and he offended the Emperor. The Emperor was greatly angered and ordered his attendants to kill him on the spot. He soon regretted it but could not overtake the deed, and therefore issued an edict condemning Wansui: 'The Pillar of State and Duke of Taiping, Wansui, was raised and entrusted with command of the army on every campaign. Formerly, when the south rebelled, he was sent to punish them. The Governor of Kunzhou, Cuan Wan, harbored treacherous intent and brought harm to the people. We had made full plans and ordered Wan brought to court. Wansui accepted much gold and silver, disobeyed the plan by keeping him, and caused Cuan Wan soon to rebel again, costing further armies before it was pacified. The authorities investigated; the crime merited extreme punishment, but We pardoned his life remembering his merit, and within a short time restored his office. Recently he again commanded the army in advance against the frontier tribes. The Turk Khan Tatou led his fierce horde intending to resist; once they saw our military might they fled at once—blades unstained, the rebels dissolved. Such a victory is a glory of the state; We wished to complete his merit and reward him again. Yet on the day the registers were submitted, Wansui and Dinghe harbored treachery, falsely claiming they had met the rebels in battle face to face and did not report the truth, cherishing schemes of reversal and mocking the laws of the state. Only one who serves with full loyalty and upright conduct, without deceit in his heart, is a good general; as for Wansui, who sought merit by fraud, he is a traitor to the state. The statutes of the court cannot be bent—we cannot spare him again.' On the day of his death, all gentlemen and commoners who heard of it, whether they knew him or not, none failed to mourn him.

units.zh: 史萬歲，京兆杜陵人也．父靜，周滄州刺史．萬歲少英武，善騎射，驍捷若飛．好讀兵書，兼精占候．年十五，值周、齊戰於芒山，萬歲時從父入軍，旗鼓正相望，萬歲令左右趣治裝急去．俄而周師大敗，其父由是奇之．武帝時，釋褐侍伯上士．及平齊之役，其父戰沒，萬歲以忠臣子，拜開府儀同三司，襲爵太平縣公．
units.en: Shi Wansui came from Duling in Jingzhao. His father Jing had been Zhou’s governor of Cangzhou. From youth Wansui was bold and martial, skilled in riding and archery, swift as if he could fly. He loved military texts and was also expert in divination and celestial signs. At fifteen, when Zhou and Qi fought at Mount Mang, he was with his father in the army. The two hosts were just facing each other when Wansui told his attendants to pack up and leave at once. Soon the Zhou army was routed, and his father marveled at him. Under Emperor Wu he entered service as senior attendant of the guard. In the pacification of Qi his father died in battle; as a loyal minister’s son, Wansui was made director of the bureau with equal standing and inherited the dukedom of Taiping county.
units.literal: Shi Wansui was a native of Duling in Jingzhao. His father Jing was Governor of Cangzhou under Zhou. Wansui from youth was heroic and martial, skilled in horsemanship and archery, swift and agile as if flying. He loved to read books of war and was also expert in divination and observation of the heavens. At fifteen, when Zhou and Qi fought at Mount Mang, Wansui was following his father into the army. The banners and drums of the two sides were just facing one another when Wansui ordered his attendants to pack up quickly and leave at once. Soon the Zhou army was utterly defeated, and his father marveled at him for this. Under Emperor Wu he first took office as Senior Attendant of the Guard. In the campaign to pacify Qi his father fell in battle; as the son of a loyal minister, Wansui was appointed Director of the Bureau with Equal Standing and inherited the title Duke of Taiping County.

units.zh: 萬歲為將，不治營伍，令士卒各隨所安，無警夜之備，虜亦不敢犯．臨陣對敵，應變無方，號為良將．有子懷義．
units.en: As a commander Wansui did not fuss over camp order; he let his men settle where they were comfortable and kept no strict night watch, yet the barbarians dared not attack him. In battle he adapted without fixed method and was accounted a fine general. He had a son named Huaiyi.
units.literal: As a general Wansui did not regulate camp formations strictly; he let the soldiers settle where they were comfortable, with no night-watch preparations, yet the barbarians also dared not attack. Facing the enemy in battle he adapted without fixed method and was called a fine general. He had a son Huaiyi.

units.zh: 爾朱勣以謀反伏誅，萬歲頗相關涉，坐除名，配敦煌為戍卒．其戍主甚驍武，每單騎深入突厥中，掠取羊馬，輒大剋獲．突厥無眾寡，莫之敢當．其人深自矜負，數罵辱萬歲．萬歲患之，自言亦有武用．戍主試令馳射而工，戍主笑曰：「小人定可．」萬歲請弓馬，復掠突厥中，大得六畜而歸．戍主始善之，每與同行，輒入突厥數百里，名讋北夷．竇榮定之擊突厥也，萬歲詣轅門請自效．榮定數聞其名，見而大悅．因遣人謂突厥曰：「士卒何罪過，令殺之，但當各遣一壯士決勝負耳．」突厥許諾，因遣一騎挑戰．榮定遣萬歲出應之，萬歲馳斬其首而還．突厥大驚，不敢復戰，遂引軍而去．由是拜上儀同，領車騎將軍．平陳之役，又以功加上開府．
units.en: Erzhu Ji was executed for treason; Wansui was somewhat implicated, stripped of rank, and sent to Dunhuang as a garrison soldier. The garrison commander was a fierce fighter who often rode alone deep into Turk lands for sheep and horses and always returned with rich spoils. No Turk band, large or small, dared face him. Proud and overbearing, he repeatedly abused Wansui. Wansui, resenting this, said he too had martial skill. The commander tested him at mounted archery and found him expert. The commander laughed, “The fellow will do.” Wansui took bow and horse, raided the Turks again, and came back with great herds. The commander then favored him and often rode with him hundreds of li into Turk territory until his name terrified the northern tribes. When Dou Rongding attacked the Turks, Wansui came to the camp gate and offered to prove himself in service. Rongding had often heard of him and was delighted. He sent word to the Turks: “What crime have ordinary soldiers committed that you kill them? Let each side send one champion to decide the matter.” The Turks agreed and sent a challenger. Rongding sent Wansui out; he galloped forward, struck off the man’s head, and returned. The Turks were terrified, would not fight again, and withdrew. For this Wansui was made director with equal standing of the first rank and general of chariots and cavalry. In the conquest of Chen he was again promoted to superior director of the bureau for his merit.
units.literal: Erzhu Ji was executed for plotting rebellion; Wansui was somewhat implicated and was stripped of rank and banished to Dunhuang as a garrison soldier. The garrison commander was very fierce in war; alone on horseback he would penetrate deep into Turk territory, seize sheep and horses, and always win great spoils. No Turk force, few or many, dared stand against him. The man was deeply proud and repeatedly abused and insulted Wansui. Wansui resented this and declared that he too had martial ability. The commander tested him with mounted archery and found him skilled. The commander laughed and said: 'The fellow will do.' Wansui asked for bow and horse, raided the Turks again, and returned with a great haul of livestock. The commander then treated him well and often went with him, penetrating several hundred li into Turk lands until his name terrified the northern barbarians. When Dou Rongding attacked the Turks, Wansui came to the camp gate and asked for a chance to prove himself in service. Rongding had often heard his name and was greatly pleased at the meeting. He therefore sent word to the Turks: 'What crime have the soldiers committed that you should kill them? Let each side send one brave man to decide the outcome.' The Turks agreed and sent one horseman to challenge. Rongding sent Wansui out to meet him; Wansui galloped forward, cut off his head, and returned. The Turks were greatly alarmed, dared not fight again, and withdrew their army. For this he was appointed Director with Equal Standing of the First Rank and made General of Chariots and Cavalry. In the campaign to pacify Chen he was again promoted to Superior Director of the Bureau for his merit.

units.zh: 顧有司曰：「明日將斬之．」萬歲懼而服罪，頓首請命．左僕射高熲、左衛大將軍元旻等進曰：「史萬歲雄略過人，每行兵用師之處，未嘗不身先士卒，尤善撫御，將士樂為致力，雖古名將未能過也．」上意少解，於是除名為民．歲餘，復官爵．尋拜河州刺史，復領行軍總管以備胡．
units.en: He turned to the officials: “Tomorrow he dies.” Wansui, terrified, confessed and begged for his life. The left vice director Gao Jiong, the general of the left guard Yuan Min, and others said, “Shi Wansui’s strategy surpasses other men; in every campaign he leads from the front. He is especially skilled at winning his men, who gladly give their all—even famous generals of old could not match him.” The emperor’s anger eased somewhat; Wansui was stripped of rank and made a commoner. After a year his titles were restored. He was soon governor of Hezhou and again commander on campaign against the barbarians.
units.literal: He turned to the officials and said: 'Tomorrow he shall be beheaded.' Wansui in fear confessed guilt and knocked his head on the ground begging for his life. The Left Vice Director Gao Jiong, the General of the Left Guard Yuan Min, and others advanced and said: 'Shi Wansui's heroic strategy surpasses other men; wherever he leads troops in campaign he has never failed to go before the soldiers in person. He is especially skilled in comforting and controlling them, and officers and men gladly exert themselves for him—even famous generals of old could not surpass him.' The Emperor's mind softened somewhat, and Wansui was therefore stripped of rank and made a commoner. After more than a year his office and titles were restored. Soon he was appointed Governor of Hezhou and again made Commander on Campaign to guard against the barbarians.

units.zh: 尉迥之亂也，萬歲從梁士彥擊之．軍次馮翊，見群雁飛來，萬歲謂士彥曰：「請射行中第三者．」既射之，應弦而落，三軍莫不悅服．及與迥軍相遇，每戰先登，鄴城之陣，官軍稍卻，萬歲謂左右曰：「事急矣，吾當破之．」於是馳馬奮擊，殺數十人，眾亦齊力，官軍乃振．及迥平，以功拜上大將軍．
units.en: During Yuchi Jiong’s rebellion Wansui followed Liang Shiyan. The army halted at Fengyi when a flock of wild geese flew past. Wansui said to Shiyan, “Let me shoot the third bird in the line.” He loosed his arrow and it fell at the twang; the whole army marveled. Whenever they met Jiong’s forces he was first over the wall. Before Ye City the imperial troops began to falter. Wansui told his men, “This is urgent—I will break them.” He spurred his horse and struck, killing dozens; his men rallied with him and the army recovered its nerve. When Jiong was subdued, Wansui was made grand general of the first rank for his merit.
units.literal: During Yuchi Jiong's rebellion Wansui followed Liang Shiyan in the attack. The army halted at Fengyi and saw a flock of wild geese flying by. Wansui said to Shiyan: 'Allow me to shoot the third bird in the line.' He shot, and it fell at the twang of the string; the whole army was pleased and submitted to him. When they met Jiong's army he was first to charge in every battle. At the battle before Ye City the government troops were wavering. Wansui said to those beside him: 'The situation is critical—I shall break them.' He then spurred his horse and struck fiercely, killing several dozen men; his troops also exerted themselves together, and the government army was rallied. When Jiong was pacified, Wansui was made Grand General of the First Rank for his merit.

units.zh: 及高智慧等作亂江南，以行軍總管從楊素擊之．萬歲率眾二千，自東陽別道而進，踰嶺越海，攻陷溪洞不可勝數．前後七百餘戰，轉鬥千餘里，寂無聲問者十旬，遠近皆以萬歲為沒．萬歲以水陸阻絕，信使不通，乃置書竹筒中，浮之於水．汲者得之，以言於素．素大悅，上其事．高祖嗟歎，賜其家錢十萬，還拜左領軍將軍．
units.en: When Gao Zhihui and others rebelled in the south, Wansui followed Yang Su as commander on campaign. With two thousand men he advanced by a separate route from Dongyang, crossed mountains and sea, and took ravine strongholds beyond count. In more than seven hundred fights over a thousand li of hills, for a hundred days no word came from him; everyone thought Wansui was dead. Cut off by land and water, he sealed a letter in a bamboo tube and set it adrift. Someone who drew water found it and told Su. Su was delighted and reported upward. Gaozu marveled and gave his family one hundred thousand cash; on his return Wansui was made general of the left forward army.
units.literal: When Gao Zhihui and others rebelled in the south, Wansui, as Commander on Campaign, followed Yang Su in the attack. Wansui led two thousand men by a separate route from Dongyang, crossed ranges and seas, and stormed ravine strongholds beyond counting. In more than seven hundred battles over a thousand li of marching hills, for a hundred days there was no word from him; near and far all thought Wansui had perished. Because land and water routes were cut off and messengers could not pass, he placed a letter in a bamboo tube and floated it on the water. One who drew water found it and reported to Su. Su was greatly pleased and submitted the matter to the throne. Gaozu sighed in admiration, granted his family one hundred thousand cash, and on his return appointed him General of the Left Forward Army.

units.zh: 先是，南寧夷爨翫來降，拜昆州刺史，既而復叛．遂以萬歲為行軍總管，率眾擊之．入自蜻蛉川，經弄凍，次小勃弄、大勃弄，至于南中．賊前後屯據要害，萬歲皆擊破之．行數百里，見諸葛亮紀功碑，銘其背曰：「萬歲之後，勝我者過此．」萬歲令左右倒其碑而進．渡西二河，入渠濫川，行千餘里，破其三十餘部，虜獲男女二萬餘口．諸夷大懼，遣使請降，獻明珠徑寸．於是勒石頌美隋德．萬歲遣使馳奏，請將翫入朝，詔許之．爨翫陰有二心，不欲詣闕，因賂萬歲以金寶，萬歲於是捨翫而還．蜀王時在益州，知其受賂，遣使將索之．萬歲聞而悉以所得金寶沉之於江，索無所獲．以功進位柱國．晉王廣虛衿敬之，待以交友之禮．上知為所善，令萬歲督晉府軍事．明年，爨翫復反，蜀王秀奏萬歲受賂縱賊，致生邊患，無大臣節．上令窮治其事，事皆驗，罪當死．上數之曰：「受金放賊，重勞士馬．朕念將士暴露，寢不安席，食不甘味，卿豈社稷臣也？」
units.en: Earlier, Cuan Wan of the Ningnan Yi had surrendered and been made governor of Kunzhou, then rebelled again. Wansui was sent as commander on campaign against him. He entered by the Qingling River, passed Nongdong, and halted at Lesser and Greater Bonong before reaching the southern heartland. The rebels held every strong point; Wansui broke them all. After several hundred li he came upon Zhuge Liang’s victory stele, inscribed on the back: “After ten thousand years, whoever surpasses me will pass this place.” Wansui had his men overturn it and march on. He crossed the two western rivers, entered the Quluan River, marched more than a thousand li, and shattered more than thirty tribes, taking more than twenty thousand captives. The Yi were terrified, sent envoys to surrender, and presented a pearl an inch across. He carved a stone praising Sui virtue. Wansui sent a swift report asking that Wan be brought to court; the edict agreed. Wan secretly had no wish to come to the capital and bribed Wansui with gold and jewels; Wansui then left him and returned. The prince of Shu was in Yizhou; learning of the bribe, he sent men to seize the goods. Wansui heard of it and sank everything he had received in the river, and nothing was found. For his merit he was made pillar of state. Prince Jin Guang treated him with open respect as a friend. The emperor, knowing Guang favored him, put Wansui in charge of the prince of Jin’s military affairs. The next year Cuan Wan rebelled again. Prince Xiu of Shu reported that Wansui had taken bribes and released the rebel, bringing border trouble and failing the integrity of a great minister. A full investigation confirmed everything; the crime merited death. The emperor recounted his offenses: “You took gold and let the rebel go, wasting soldiers and horses. When I think of men exposed in the field I cannot sleep or eat with ease—are you a minister of the altars of state?”
units.literal: Earlier, Cuan Wan of the Ningnan Yi had come to surrender and was appointed Governor of Kunzhou, but soon rebelled again. Wansui was therefore made Commander on Campaign and led troops to attack him. He entered by the Qingling River, passed through Nongdong, halted at Lesser Bonong and Greater Bonong, and reached the southern center. The rebels held key points before and behind; Wansui defeated them all. After marching several hundred li he saw Zhuge Liang's stele commemorating merit, inscribed on the reverse: 'After ten thousand years, whoever surpasses me will pass this place.' Wansui ordered his attendants to overturn the stele and advance. He crossed the two western rivers, entered the Quluan River, marched more than a thousand li, and broke more than thirty tribes, capturing more than twenty thousand men and women. The various Yi were greatly afraid, sent envoys to surrender, and presented a pearl an inch across. He then carved a stone praising Sui virtue. Wansui sent a messenger post-haste to report and request that Wan be brought to court; the edict approved. Wan secretly had other intentions and did not wish to go to the capital; he therefore bribed Wansui with gold and jewels, and Wansui thereupon left Wan and returned. The Prince of Shu was then in Yizhou; learning of the bribe, he sent men to seize the goods. When Wansui heard of it he sank all the gold and jewels he had received in the river, and nothing could be found. For his merit he was promoted to Pillar of State. Prince Jin Guang treated him with open respect and the courtesy due a friend. The Emperor, knowing Guang favored him, ordered Wansui to supervise the military affairs of the Prince of Jin's establishment. The next year Cuan Wan rebelled again. Prince Xiu of Shu memorialized that Wansui had taken bribes and released the rebel, causing border trouble and lacking the integrity of a great minister. The Emperor ordered a full investigation; the facts were all verified and the crime merited death. The Emperor counted his offenses, saying: 'You took gold and released the rebel, greatly wasting soldiers and horses. When I think of the troops exposed in the field I cannot sleep peacefully or eat with pleasure—are you a minister of the altars of state?'

units.zh: 萬歲曰：「臣留爨翫者，恐其州有變，留以鎮撫．臣還至瀘水，詔書方到，由是不將入朝，實不受賂．」上以萬歲心有欺隱，大怒曰：「朕以卿為好人，何乃官高祿重，翻為國賊也？」
units.en: Wansui said, “I left Cuan Wan because I feared unrest in his prefecture and kept him to pacify the region. When I reached the Lu River your edict had only just arrived, so I did not bring him in. I truly took no bribe.” The emperor, believing he was deceitful, raged: “I thought you a good man—how, with high rank and rich pay, have you become a traitor to the state?”
units.literal: Wansui said: 'Your servant left Cuan Wan because I feared trouble in his prefecture and kept him to pacify and reassure the region. When I returned to the Lu River the edict had only just arrived; therefore I did not bring him to court. I truly did not accept a bribe.' The Emperor, believing Wansui harbored deceit in his heart, was greatly angered and said: 'I took you for a good man—how is it that with high office and heavy emolument you have turned into a traitor to the state?'

units.zh: 子幹西涉青海，北臨玄塞，胡夷懾憚，烽候無警，亦有可稱．萬歲實懷智勇，善撫士卒，人皆樂死，師不疲勞．北卻匈奴，南平夷、獠，兵鋒所指，威驚絕域．論功仗氣，犯忤貴臣，偏聽生姦，死非其罪，人皆痛惜，有李廣之風焉．劉方號令無私，治軍嚴肅，克剪林邑，遂清南海，徼外百蠻，無思不服．凡此諸將，志烈過人，出當推轂之重，入受爪牙之寄，雖馬伏波之威行南裔，趙充國之聲動西羌，語事論功，各一時也．
units.en: Zigan crossed the Qinghai westward and faced the dark northern passes; the tribes feared him and the beacons knew no alarm—this too deserves praise. Wansui truly had wisdom and courage, won his soldiers’ hearts, and every man gladly faced death; his armies never tired. In the north he drove back the Xiongnu; in the south he pacified the Yi and Liao; wherever his blades pointed, his might shook the farthest lands. When merit was debated he spoke with proud spirit, offended powerful ministers, partial listening bred treachery, and he died for a crime not his own—all mourned him, and he had something of Li Guang about him. Liu Fang’s orders were impartial; he governed the army with severity, cut down Linyi, and cleared the southern sea; the hundred tribes beyond the borders all wished to submit. All these generals had wills and valor beyond ordinary men: abroad they bore the weight of the realm’s defense, at home they were the emperor’s trusted claws and teeth. Though Ma Yuan, the General Who Pacifies the Waves, carried his might through the south and Zhao Chongguo’s fame shook the western Qiang, speaking of deeds and weighing merit, each was foremost in his time.
units.literal: Zigan crossed the Qinghai in the west and faced the dark frontier passes in the north; the Hu and Yi feared him and the beacon fires knew no alarm—this too is praiseworthy. Wansui truly possessed wisdom and courage, was skilled in comforting soldiers, and every man gladly faced death; his armies knew no fatigue. In the north he drove back the Xiongnu; in the south he pacified the Yi and Liao; wherever his blades pointed, his might astonished the farthest lands. When merit was debated he spoke with proud spirit, offended powerful ministers, partial listening bred treachery, and he died for a crime not his own—all mourned him, and he had the air of Li Guang. Liu Fang's orders were without favoritism; he governed the army with severity, cut down Linyi, and cleared the southern sea; the hundred barbarians beyond the borders all wished to submit. All these generals had wills and valor surpassing other men: abroad they bore the weight of the chariot-pusher's trust, at home they received the charge of the ruler's claws and teeth. Though Ma Yuan, the General Who Pacifies the Waves, extended his might through the southern regions and Zhao Chongguo's fame shook the western Qiang, speaking of deeds and weighing merit, each was foremost in his age.

units.zh: 開皇末，突厥達頭可汗犯塞，上令晉王廣及楊素出靈武道，漢王諒與萬歲出馬邑道．[一]萬歲率柱國張定和、大將軍李藥王、楊義臣等出塞，至大斤山，與虜相遇．達頭遣使問曰：「隋將為誰？」
units.en: At the end of Kaihuang the Turk khan Tatou raided the frontier. The emperor sent Prince Jin Guang and Yang Su by the Lingwu route, and Prince Han Liang and Wansui by the Mayi route. [1] Wansui led the pillars of state Zhang Dinghe and the grand generals Li Yaowang, Yang Yichen, and others beyond the border. At Mount Dajin they met the enemy. Tatou sent a messenger to ask, “Who is the Sui general?”
units.literal: At the end of Kaihuang the Turk Khan Tatou violated the border. The Emperor ordered Prince Jin Guang and Yang Su to go out by the Lingwu route, and Prince Han Liang and Wansui by the Mayi route. [1] Wansui led the Pillars of State Zhang Dinghe, the Grand Generals Li Yaowang, Yang Yichen, and others beyond the border. At Mount Dajin they met the barbarians. Tatou sent a messenger to ask: 'Who is the Sui general?'

units.zh: 候騎報「史萬歲也」．突厥復問曰：「得非敦煌戍卒乎？」
units.en: The scouts answered, “Shi Wansui.” The Turks asked again, “Is he not the garrison soldier from Dunhuang?”
units.literal: The scouts reported, 'It is Shi Wansui.' The Turks asked again: 'Can it be the garrison soldier from Dunhuang?'

units.zh: 周宣嗣位，不率典章，衣褘翟、稱中宮者，凡有五。
units.en: When Emperor Xuan of Northern Zhou succeeded to the throne, he did not follow the canonical regulations: five women in all wore the empress's hui and di robes and were styled ladies of the Central Palace.
units.literal: When Xuan of Zhou succeeded to the throne, he did not follow the statutes; those who wore the hui and di robes and were called Central Palace numbered five in all.

units.zh: 后姊為周明帝后，長女為周宣帝后，貴戚之盛，莫與為比，而后每謙卑自守，世以為賢。
units.en: Her elder sister was empress to Emperor Ming of Northern Zhou, and her eldest daughter became empress to Emperor Xuan; no consort kin in the realm was more exalted. Yet the empress always kept herself humble and restrained, and the world regarded her as worthy.
units.literal: The empress's elder sister was empress to Ming of Zhou, and her eldest daughter was empress to Xuan of Zhou; no kin by marriage was more exalted, yet the empress always kept herself humble and restrained, and the age considered her worthy.

units.zh: 及周宣帝崩，高祖居禁中，總百揆，后使人謂高祖曰：「大事已然，騎獸之勢，必不得下，勉之！」
units.en: When Emperor Xuan of Northern Zhou died, Emperor Wen remained within the palace and took charge of all government affairs. The empress sent word to him: "The decisive moment has come. Once you are mounted on a beast, you cannot dismount—press forward!"
units.literal: When Xuan of Zhou died, the Founding Emperor dwelt in the forbidden precincts and oversaw all affairs of state. The empress sent someone to tell him: "The great matter is already settled. Once you are mounted on a beast, you cannot come down—press on!"

units.zh: 異既走險，迪又逃刑，誑侮王人，為之川藪，遂使袁熙請席，遠歎頭行，馬援觀蛙，猶安井底。
units.en: Yi had fled to the hills and Di had escaped justice. They mocked the king's officers and made a mountain lair—like Yuan Xi asking for a mat and sighing at Touxing far away, like Ma Yuan watching frogs content in a well.
units.literal: Yi had already fled to peril and Di had escaped punishment; they deceived and insulted the king's men and made themselves a mountain lair—so Yuan Xi asked for a mat and sighed far off at Touxing's march, and Ma Yuan watched frogs yet was content in the well bottom.

units.zh: 故司空歐陽公，昔有表奏，請宣薄伐，遙途意合，若伏波之論兵，長逝遺誠，同子顏之勿赦。
units.en: The late minister of works Lord Ouyang once memorialized for a limited campaign; his intent matched ours across the distance, like Fubo's talk of war. Dead, he left a charge like Ziyan's "do not spare."
units.literal: The late minister of works Lord Ouyang in old days had a memorial asking to proclaim a limited campaign; across the distance his intent matched, like Fubo on warfare; long gone he left a testament, the same as Ziyan's "do not spare."

units.zh: 及叔陵之肆逆也，事既不捷，出據東府，申馳召右衛蕭摩訶帥兵先至，追斬之，因入城中，收其府庫，後主深嘉之。
units.en: When Shuling's violent outrage took place, the affair did not succeed and he went out to hold the eastern palace; Shen galloped to summon right guard Xiao Mohe to lead troops and arrive first, pursued and beheaded him, then entered the city and seized his treasury stores—Houzhu deeply commended him.
units.literal: When Shuling's violent outrage took place, the affair did not succeed and he went out to hold the eastern palace; Shen galloped to summon Right Guard Xiao Mohe to lead troops and arrive first, pursued and beheaded him, then entered the city and seized his treasury stores—Houzhu deeply commended him.

units.zh: 杜彥，雲中人也。
units.en: Du Yan was from Yunzhong.
units.literal: Du Yan—Du Yan was a native of Yunzhong.

units.zh: 後數日，上曰：「吾思可以鎮榆林者，莫過杜彥。」
units.en: A few days later he said, "When I think who should hold Yulin, no one surpasses Du Yan."
units.literal: Several days later the emperor said: "When I consider who could guard Yulin, none surpasses Du Yan."

units.zh: 彥性勇果，善騎射。
units.en: Yan was bold and decisive by nature and excelled at horseback archery.
units.literal: Yan by nature was brave and resolute, skilled in mounted archery.

units.zh: 軍至南陵，賊屯據江岸，彥遣儀同樊子蓋率精兵擊破其柵，獲船六百餘艘。
units.en: At Nanling the enemy held the riverbank; Yan sent Yitong Fan Zigai with an elite force to break their stockade and capture more than six hundred vessels.
units.literal: When the army reached Nanling, the enemy held the riverbank; Yan sent Yitong Fan Zigai at the head of picked troops to smash their palisade and seize more than six hundred boats.

units.zh: 智慧餘黨往往屯聚，保投溪洞，彥水陸兼進，攻錦山、陽父、若、石壁四洞，悉平之，皆斬其渠帥。
units.en: Zhihui's scattered followers held out in mountain ravines; Yan struck by land and water, reduced the strongholds at Jinshan, Yangfu, Ruo, and Shibi, and executed their leaders.
units.literal: Zhihui's remaining partisans often gathered and took refuge in stream caves; Yan advanced by land and water, attacked the four lairs of Jinshan, Yangfu, Ruo, and Shibi, pacified them all, and beheaded their chieftains.

units.zh: 賊李陀擁眾數千，據彭山，彥襲擊破之，斬陀，傳其首。
units.en: The rebel Li Tuo gathered several thousand men on Pengshan; Yan surprised and routed him, killed Tuo, and forwarded his head.
units.literal: The bandit Li Tuo mustered several thousand men and held Pengshan; Yan raided and defeated him, beheaded Tuo, and sent his head to the capital.

units.zh: 突厥來寇，彥輒擒斬之，北夷畏憚，胡馬不敢至塞。
units.en: Whenever Turks raided, Yan captured and executed them; the northern peoples stood in awe of him, and their horsemen no longer dared approach the border.
units.literal: When the Turks came to raid, Yan would capture and behead them; the northern barbarians feared him, and Turkic horses dared not approach the frontier.

units.zh: 明年，拜隴州刺史，賜爵永安縣伯。
units.en: The following year he became prefect of Longzhou and was created Baron of Yong'an.
units.literal: The next year he was appointed prefect of Longzhou and ennobled as Baron of Yong'an county.

units.zh: 進位上開府，改封襄武縣侯，拜魏郡太守。
units.en: He was promoted to Senior Commander-in-Chief, enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiangwu, and appointed administrator of Wei commandery.
units.literal: He was advanced to Senior Commander-in-Chief, his fief changed to Marquis of Xiangwu county, and he was appointed administrator of Wei commandery.

units.zh: 及陳平，賜物五千段，粟六千石，進位柱國，賜子寶安爵昌陽縣公。
units.en: After Chen fell he received five thousand bolts of goods and six thousand piculs of grain, was promoted to Pillar of State, and his son Bao'an was created Duke of Changyang.
units.literal: When Chen was pacified, he was granted five thousand bolts of goods and six thousand piculs of grain, advanced to Pillar of State, and his son Bao'an was ennobled as Duke of Changyang county.

units.zh: 仕周，釋褐左侍上士，後從柱國陸通擊陳將吳明徹於土州，破之。
units.en: He entered Zhou service as Left Attendant Senior Clerk and later followed Pillar of State Lu Tong to attack the Chen general Wu Mingche at Tuzhou and rout him.
units.literal: He served Zhou, upon first appointment becoming Left Attendant Senior Clerk; later he followed the pillar of state Lu Tong in attacking the Chen general Wu Mingche at Tuzhou and defeated him.

units.zh: 平陳之役，以行軍總管與新義公韓擒相繼而進。
units.en: During the conquest of Chen he served as campaign commander, advancing in concert with Duke of Xinyi Han Qin.
units.literal: In the campaign to pacify Chen, as campaign commander he advanced in succession with the Duke of Xinyi, Han Qin.

units.zh: 十八年，遼東之役，以行軍總管從漢王至營州。
units.en: In the eighteenth year, during the Liaodong campaign, he served as campaign commander under the Prince of Han and marched to Yingzhou.
units.literal: In the eighteenth year, in the Liaodong campaign, as campaign commander he followed the Prince of Han to Yingzhou.

units.zh: 尋遷儀同，治隆山郡事。
units.en: He was soon promoted to Yitong and put in charge of Longshan commandery.
units.literal: Soon he was transferred to Yitong and administered the affairs of Longshan commandery.

units.zh: 拜洪州總管，甚有治名。
units.en: Appointed regional commander of Hongzhou, he earned a strong reputation for effective administration.
units.literal: He was appointed regional commander of Hongzhou and gained a great reputation for good governance.

units.zh: 後六歲，征為左武衛將軍。
units.en: Six years later he was recalled to the capital as general of the Left Martial Guard.
units.literal: Six years later he was summoned to serve as general of the Left Martial Guard.

units.zh: 父遷，屬葛榮之亂，徙家於幽。
units.en: During Ge Rong's rebellion, his father Qian relocated the household to Youzhou.
units.literal: His father Qian, during Ge Rong's rebellion, moved the family to You.

units.zh: 後數年，朝廷複追錄前功，賜子寶虔爵承縣公。
units.en: Some years later the court again recorded his earlier merit and created his son Baoqian Duke of Cheng.
units.literal: Several years later the court again recorded his earlier merit and ennobled his son Baoqian as Duke of Cheng county.

units.zh: 子寶虔，大業末，文城郡丞。
units.en: His son Baoqian served late in the Daye era as assistant administrator of Wencheng commandery.
units.literal: His son Baoqian, at the end of the Daye era, was assistant administrator of Wencheng commandery.

units.zh: 開皇初，授丹州刺史，進爵為公。
units.en: Early in the Kaihuang era he was made prefect of Danzhou and raised to ducal rank.
units.literal: At the beginning of Kaihuang he was appointed prefect of Danzhou and advanced in rank to duke.

units.zh: 又擊叛蠻，克倉塠、白楊二柵，並斬其渠帥。
units.en: He also campaigned against rebel tribes, took the stockades at Cangdui and Baiyang, and executed their leaders.
units.literal: He again attacked rebel barbarians, captured the two stockades of Cangdui and Baiyang, and beheaded their chieftains.

units.zh: 進平郢州賊帥樊志，以戰功拜大都督。
units.en: He advanced to suppress the Yingzhou rebel Fan Zhi and, for his victories, was appointed Grand Commander.
units.literal: Advancing, he pacified the Yingzhou bandit leader Fan Zhi and, for battle merit, was appointed Grand Commander.

units.zh: 高祖為丞相，從韋孝寬擊尉迥於相州，每戰有功，賜物三千段，奴婢三十口。
units.en: While Gaozu was still chief minister, he followed Wei Xiaokuan against Yuchi Jiong at Xiangzhou, distinguishing himself in every engagement and receiving three thousand bolts of goods and thirty slaves.
units.literal: When Emperor Gaozu was chief minister, he followed Wei Xiaokuan in attacking Yuchi Jiong at Xiangzhou; in every battle he had merit, and was granted three thousand bolts of goods and thirty household slaves.

units.zh: 進至新林，與擒合軍。
units.en: He pushed on to Xinlin and joined forces with Han Qin.
units.literal: Advancing to Xinlin, he united his forces with Qin's.

units.zh: 渡江，擊南陵城，拔之，擒其守將許翼。
units.en: He crossed the Yangzi, stormed Nanling, took the city, and captured its commander Xu Yi.
units.literal: Crossing the river, he attacked Nanling city, took it, and captured its defending general Xu Yi.

units.zh: 高智慧等之作亂也，複以行軍總管從楊素討之，別解江州圍。
units.en: When Gao Zhihui and others rebelled, he again served as campaign commander under Yang Su and on his own broke the siege of Jiangzhou.
units.literal: When Gao Zhihui and others rose in rebellion, he again served as campaign commander following Yang Su to suppress them and separately lifted the siege of Jiangzhou.

units.zh: 又擊徐州、宜豐二洞，悉平之。
units.en: He also subdued the rebel bases at Xuzhou and Yifeng.
units.literal: He again attacked the two lairs of Xuzhou and Yifeng and pacified them completely.

units.zh: 賜奴婢百餘口。
units.en: He was rewarded with more than a hundred slaves.
units.literal: He was granted more than a hundred household slaves.

units.zh: 於是征拜雲州總管。
units.en: He was then recalled and appointed regional commander of Yunzhou.
units.literal: Thereupon he was summoned and appointed regional commander of Yunzhou.

units.zh: 突厥複寇雲州，上令楊素擊走之，是後猶恐為邊患，以彥素為突厥所憚，複拜雲州總管。
units.en: When the Turks raided Yunzhou again, the emperor sent Yang Su to repel them; still anxious about the frontier, and knowing the Turks feared Yan, he reappointed him commander of Yunzhou.
units.literal: The Turks again raided Yunzhou; the emperor ordered Yang Su to drive them off. Still fearing border trouble afterward, and because Yan had long been feared by the Turks, he was again appointed regional commander of Yunzhou.

units.zh: 上以彥曉習軍旅，令總統五十營事。
units.en: Knowing Yan's mastery of military affairs, the emperor put him in overall charge of fifty camps.
units.literal: Because the emperor knew Yan was versed in military affairs, he ordered him to oversee the affairs of fifty camps.

units.zh: 及還，拜朔州總管。
units.en: On his return he was appointed regional commander of Shuozhou.
units.literal: Upon his return he was appointed regional commander of Shuozhou.

units.zh: 未幾，以疾征還，卒，時年六十。
units.en: Soon afterward he was recalled because of illness and died at sixty.
units.literal: Before long, recalled on account of illness, he died at the age of sixty.

units.zh: 州縣上其事，上遣平昌公宇文弼詣其家勞問之。
units.en: The prefecture and county reported this to the court; the emperor sent Duke of Pingchang Yuwen Bi to visit their home and commend them and inquire after their welfare.
units.literal: The prefecture and county reported this to the court; the emperor sent Duke of Pingchang Yuwen Bi to visit their home and extend commendation and inquiries.

units.zh: 又京兆人達奚通有妾王氏善歌，貴遊宴聚，多或要致，於是輾轉亦出入王家。
units.en: Moreover Daxi Tong of Jingzhao had a concubine, Lady Wang, skilled in song; at banquets of the noble and powerful many would request her, and so by turns she also came and went at Zheng's residence.
units.literal: Moreover Daxi Tong of Jingzhao had a concubine, Lady Wang, skilled in song; at banquets of the noble and powerful many would request her presence, and so by turns she also came and went at the prince's residence.

units.zh: 晟先知攝圖、玷厥、阿波、突利等叔侄兄弟各統強兵，俱號可汗，分居四面，內懷猜忌，外示和同，難以力征，易可離間，因上書曰：「臣聞喪亂之極，必致升平，是故上天啟其機，聖人成其務。
units.en: Sheng had long known that Shetu, Dianjue, Abo, Tuli, and other kinsmen each commanded powerful forces, all called themselves qaghan, and held separate domains on four sides; inwardly suspicious yet outwardly cordial, they could not easily be crushed by force but could readily be divided; he therefore memorialized, "I have heard that the depth of disorder must give way to great peace, and that Heaven opens the moment for the sage to complete the work.
units.literal: Sheng had already known that Shetu, Dianjue, Abo, Tuli, and others—these uncles, nephews, and brothers—each commanded strong armies, all styled themselves qaghan, and held separate domains on four sides; inwardly they harbored suspicion, outwardly they showed harmony; they could not easily be overcome by force, but might readily be set at odds; he therefore submitted a memorial saying, "Your servant has heard that the extreme of disorder must lead to great peace; therefore Heaven opens the opportunity and the sage completes the task.

units.zh: 玷厥之於攝圖，兵強而位下，外名相屬，內隙已彰，鼓動其情，必將自戰。
units.en: Dianjue stands to Shetu with strong forces but inferior rank; though linked in name, the breach within is already plain, and if their passions are provoked they will turn on each other.
units.literal: Dianjue toward Shetu has strong troops but a lower position; outwardly they are joined in name, but inwardly the rift is already clear; if their passions are stirred, they will surely fight one another.

units.zh: 因遣太僕元暉出伊吾道，使詣玷厥，賜以狼頭纛，謬為欽敬，禮數甚優。
units.en: He therefore dispatched the Master of the Imperial Stud Yuan Hui by the Yiwu route to Dianjue, presenting a wolf-head banner and treating him with exaggerated respect and lavish ceremony.
units.literal: He therefore sent the Master of the Imperial Stud Yuan Hui by the Yiwu road as envoy to Dianjue, presenting a wolf-head banner and feigning deep respect, with ceremonial honors very generous.

units.zh: 玷厥不從，引兵而去。
units.en: Dianjue refused to join him and withdrew with his forces.
units.literal: Dianjue would not follow and led his troops away.

units.zh: 阿波還無所歸，西奔玷厥，乞師十余萬，東擊攝圖，複得故地，收散卒數萬，與攝圖相攻。
units.en: Abo, with nowhere to turn, fled west to Dianjue and borrowed more than a hundred thousand men; marching east he struck Shetu, recovered his old lands, rallied tens of thousands of scattered troops, and fought him again.
units.literal: Abo returned with nowhere to go, fled west to Dianjue, and begged more than a hundred thousand troops; marching east he attacked Shetu, recovered his old territory, gathered several tens of thousands of scattered soldiers, and fought Shetu.

units.zh: 阿波使至，晟又謂之曰：「今達頭與隋連和，而攝圖不能制。
units.en: When Abo's envoy came, Sheng told him further, "Datou is now allied with Sui, yet Shetu cannot restrain him.
units.literal: When Abo's envoy arrived, Sheng again said to him, "Now Datou is allied with Sui, yet Shetu cannot control him.

units.zh: 可汗何不依附天子，連結達頭，相合為強，此萬全之計。
units.en: Why not submit to the Son of Heaven and join with Datou? Together you would be formidable—this is the sure course.
units.literal: Why does the qaghan not attach himself to the Son of Heaven and join with Datou? United you would be strong—this is a plan of complete security.

units.zh: 今宜遠交而近攻，離強而合弱，通使玷厥，說合阿波，則攝圖回兵，自防右地。
units.en: The policy now should be to ally with those far off and strike those near, to separate the strong and unite the weak: send envoys to Dianjue and draw Abo to our side, and Shetu will have to wheel his army back to defend the west.
units.literal: Now one should befriend those far and attack those near, divide the strong and unite the weak, send envoys to Dianjue and win Abo over—then Shetu will turn his army back to guard his western domain.

units.zh: 玷厥使來，引居攝圖使上。
units.en: When Dianjue's envoy arrived, he was seated above Shetu's envoy.
units.literal: When Dianjue's envoy came, he was given precedence above Shetu's envoy.

units.zh: 齊遣其歷陽王步騎五萬來援，[1]於小峴築城，法抃遣左衛將軍樊毅分兵於大峴禦之，大破齊軍，盡獲人馬器械。
units.en: Qi sent fifty thousand infantry and cavalry from the Prince of Liyang to relieve the city. [1] They built a fort at Minor Xiao. Faqu sent Left Guard General Fan Yi with a detachment to Great Xiao, shattered the Qi army, and took all their men, horses, and gear.
units.literal: Qi sent the Prince of Liyang's infantry and cavalry, fifty thousand strong, to relieve the city, and at Minor Xiao they built a fort; Faqu sent Left Guard General Fan Yi with a detachment to Great Xiao to meet them, inflicted a great defeat on Qi troops, and captured all men, horses, and equipment.

units.zh: 達奚長儒字富仁，代人也．祖俟，魏定州刺史．父慶，驃騎大將軍、儀同三司．長儒少懷節操，膽烈過人．十五，襲爵樂安公．魏大統中，起家奉車都尉．周太祖引為親信，以質直恭勤，授子都督．數有戰功，假輔國將軍，累遷使持節、撫軍將軍、通直散騎常侍．平蜀之役，恒為先鋒，攻城野戰，所當必破之．除車騎大將軍、儀同三司，增邑三百戶．天和中，除渭南郡守，遷驃騎大將軍、開府儀同三司．從武帝平齊，遷上開府，進爵成安郡公，邑千二百戶，別封一子縣公．宣政元年，除左前軍勇猛中大夫．後與烏丸軌圍陳將吳明徹於呂梁，陳遣驍將劉景率勁勇七千來為聲援，軌令長儒逆拒之．長儒於是取車輪數百，繫以大石，沉之清水，連轂相次，以待景軍．景至，船艦礙輪不得進．長儒乃縱奇兵，水陸俱發，大破之，俘數千人．及獲吳明徹，以功進位大將軍．尋授行軍總管，北巡沙塞，卒與虜遇，接戰，大破之．
units.en: Daxi Changru, styled Furen, came from Dai. His grandfather Si had been Wei’s inspector of Dingzhou; his father Qing held the ranks of general of agile cavalry and director of the three departments with equal standing. Even as a young man Changru was known for moral resolve and a daring that outstripped ordinary men. At fifteen he succeeded to the dukedom of Le’an. Under the Great Unity reign of Wei he entered service as commandant of the imperial carriages. Emperor Taizu of Zhou took him into his personal trust, and for his plainspoken loyalty and tireless diligence he received a sub-commandant’s commission. Battle honors followed in number; he was acting general who supports the state, then rose through commissioner bearing the staff, general who pacifies the army, and regular attendant-in-ordinary of the scattered cavalry. In the conquest of Shu he was always in the van—whether in siege or in the field, whatever he struck gave way. He was made general of chariots and cavalry and director of the three departments with equal standing, with three hundred added households in his fief. In the Tianhe period he became administrator of Weinan commandery, then general of agile cavalry and director of a bureau with equal standing. He followed Emperor Wu in the pacification of Qi, was promoted to superior director of the bureau, advanced to duke of Cheng’an with twelve hundred households, and had one son enfeoffed separately as a county duke. In the first year of Xuanzheng he was appointed valiant grand master of the left forward army. Later, with Wuwan Gui, he besieged the Chen commander Wu Mingche at Lüliang. Chen dispatched the fierce general Liu Jing with seven thousand elite troops in relief; Gui ordered Changru to intercept them. Changru took hundreds of cartwheels, lashed heavy stones to them, and sank them in the clear current so that hub followed hub in a barrier across the river. When Jing arrived, his fleet fouled on the wheels and could not pass. Changru then loosed his strike force by land and water together and broke the enemy, taking several thousand prisoners. After Wu Mingche fell into their hands, Changru was promoted to grand general for his achievement. He was soon made commander on campaign and patrolled the northern sands; he suddenly met the barbarians in battle and crushed them.
units.literal: Daxi Changru, courtesy name Furen, was a native of Dai. His grandfather Si served as Regional Inspector of Dingzhou under Wei. His father Qing was General of Agile Cavalry and Director of the Three Departments with Equal Standing. From youth Changru cherished integrity of character and courage that surpassed other men. At fifteen he inherited the title Duke of Le'an. In the Great Unity era of Wei he first took office as Commandant of the Imperial Carriages. Emperor Taizu of Zhou drew him into his inner circle; for his straightforward, respectful diligence he was made a sub-commandant. He won battle honors repeatedly, was provisionally made General Who Supports the State, and was promoted in succession to Commissioner Bearing the Staff, General Who Pacifies the Army, and Regular Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Scattered Cavalry. In the campaign to pacify Shu he was constantly in the vanguard; whether storming cities or fighting in the field, wherever he went he invariably broke the enemy. He was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry and Director of the Three Departments with Equal Standing, with three hundred additional households in his fief. In the Tianhe era he was made Administrator of Weinan Commandery, then promoted to General of Agile Cavalry and Director of the Bureau with Equal Standing. When he followed Emperor Wu in pacifying Qi he was promoted to Superior Director of the Bureau, advanced to Duke of Cheng'an Commandery with a fief of twelve hundred households, and one son was separately enfeoffed as a county duke. In the first year of Xuanzheng he was appointed Valiant Grand Master of the Left Forward Army. Later, together with Wuwan Gui, he besieged the Chen general Wu Mingche at Lüliang. Chen sent the fierce general Liu Jing at the head of seven thousand picked troops as a relief force. Gui ordered Changru to meet and repel them. Changru then took several hundred cart wheels, bound great stones to them, and sank them in the clear water in a continuous chain of hubs to await Jing's army. When Jing arrived, his ships struck the wheels and could not advance. Changru then unleashed his special troops, attacking by land and water together, and routed them completely, taking several thousand prisoners. When Wu Mingche was captured, Changru was promoted to Grand General for his merit. Soon afterward he was appointed Commander on Campaign and patrolled the northern desert frontier; he suddenly encountered the barbarians, joined battle, and defeated them utterly.
